<reason>Both sides built coherent, well-structured cases around the same core clash: which darkness (morning vs. evening) is more costly once the switch is abolished. CON's strongest original contribution was the collective-action framing — that a legal mandate can solve a coordination problem (getting evening light) that voluntary institutional shifts cannot, while morning darkness is a single, schedulable fix (school start times). This was a genuinely sharp point that PRO never fully neutralized, only gesturing at "Spain/Germany already do this" without engaging the coordination-failure logic directly. However, PRO's biological/circadian argument survived the exchange largely intact: CON's attempt to reduce it to "mere scheduling backlash" was answered convincingly by PRO's "revealed preference" reframing, which CON did not revisit. The decisive moment came from PRO's pressure question forcing CON to commit to a concrete threshold ("something like 8:30" as a defensible latest sunrise). CON then claimed Berlin and Warsaw sit "close to that line," directly contradicting figures PRO had already put on the record (Berlin ~9:15, Warsaw worse) — and CON never corrected or defended this inconsistency, leaving PRO's closing hammer ("the standard was doing the honest work and the conclusion was doing the wishing") uncontested and rhetorically devastating. PRO's rebuttal was clipped for length, which is a real execution cost, but the core content landed before the cut. On balance, PRO's closing more cleanly resolved the decisive numeric clash and left CON's central quantitative claim unrepaired.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's pressure question forcing CON to name a specific sunrise threshold (8:30), followed by PRO's closing showing Berlin/Warsaw under permanent DST actually land past 9:00 — a threshold CON itself set and then failed to reconcile with its own examples.</best_rebuttal>
